articles.title: Yes, North America gets a solar eclipse on Aug. 12. Here's where and when to see it
articles.excerpt: The Aug. 12 eclipse won't rival 2024's Great American Eclipse, but millions across the U.S. and Canada will still see the moon take a bite out of the sun.
articles.body: It's hardly a "Great American Eclipse," but on Aug. 12, 2026, some parts of the North American continent will see a partial solar eclipse. Will it be as impressive as on April 8, 2024 , when totality visited Mexico, 15 U.S. states and six provinces in Canada? No, yet in some parts of the U.S. and Canada, astronomers will be out in force to capture a significant chunk of the sun as it is obscured by the new moon. The spotlight may be on the total solar eclipse in Greenland, Iceland, and Spain, but millions across North America can still see the moon take a bite out of the sun on Aug. 12. The farther northeast you are, the deeper the eclipse. Here's everything you need to know about the partial solar eclipse in North America.

articles.title: I open-sourced the math behind my dividend calculator
articles.excerpt: When I built a free dividend payout calculator, the interesting part wasn't the UI — it was the math. Dividend yield, payout ratio, and especially the way a DRIP (dividend reinvestment plan) compounds…
articles.body: When I built a free dividend payout calculator , the interesting part wasn't the UI — it was the math. Dividend yield, payout ratio, and especially the way a DRIP (dividend reinvestment plan) compounds year over year. So I pulled the formulas out into a tiny, zero-dependency TypeScript library: dividend-math . This post is the story of the library and the one calculation that surprised me: how reinvestment plus growth quietly outruns a flat high yield. The library dividend-math is one file of pure functions. No runtime dependencies, no I/O, fully tree-shakeable. You can npm install dividend-math or just copy src/dividend.ts into your project.

articles.title: I outgrew nohup, so I built a daemonless job manager
articles.excerpt: I've long used nohup for background processes that I want to run independently of the terminal. These types of jobs are usually long-running, sometimes launched over an SSH connection, and often have…
articles.body: I've long used nohup for background processes that I want to run independently of the terminal. These types of jobs are usually long-running, sometimes launched over an SSH connection, and often have dependencies on other jobs. I built Jobman to combine the simplicity of nohup with features I previously wrote one-off shell scripts for, including: retries timeouts dependencies between jobs email or webhook notifications on completion or failure separate stdout and stderr logging with a combined observed-order view Jobman does this with a small per-job supervisor process; there's no shared daemon to run. It uses SQLite for job and run metadata and plain files for log storage. It's intended to be a local, per-user tool, not a system-wide or distributed scheduler.

articles.title: Sega Is Auctioning Off Shadow The Hedgehog's Real-Life Motorcycle For a Good Cause
articles.excerpt: Sega is auctioning off Shadow the Hedgehog’s real-life Dark Rider motorcycle and giving the proceeds to charity.
articles.body: Sega is auctioning off Shadow the Hedgehog’s real-life Dark Rider motorcycle and giving the proceeds to charity. Shadow the Hedgehog finally got his time to shine in the Sonic 3 movie, where he faced off against Sonic, Knuckles, and Tails in an explosive adventure that dominated the box office. To promote the character, Sega launched a campaign called 2024 Fearless: Year of Shadow, which saw the developer commission a custom motorcycle themed after the antihero that appeared at events like Gamescom to advertise his silver screen debut. Manufactured by Bourget's Bike Works in collaboration with Sega, Oil Sweat & Gears, and Atmospherics SFX, the bike is different from the one that appears in the movie, though it sports Shadow’s signature red-and black-color scheme and iconic symbol.

articles.title: SpaceX serious about building factories on the moon: 'It’s going to happen,' Elon Musk says
articles.excerpt: SpaceX plans to build factories on the moon, using robots to do much of the heavy lifting, Elon Musk said on Tuesday (Aug. 4) during SpaceX's first-ever quarterly earnings call.
articles.body: As usual, SpaceX is dreaming big. The company plans to build factories on the moon , using robots to do much of the heavy lifting, Elon Musk said on Tuesday (Aug. 4) during SpaceX 's first-ever quarterly earnings call. "We are going to land a lot of tonnage on the moon," he said. "We're going to build the factories on the moon. The robots will be helpful with that." This is not a newly revealed vision; Musk first laid it out in February, in a blog post that announced SpaceX's purchase of xAI, a company that the billionaire entrepreneur founded in 2023. But Musk doubled down on it this week, showing investors that off-Earth manufacturing is very much front-of-mind for SpaceX. The factories in question will build SpaceX's Starmind AI satellites, if all goes according to plan.
